tags.gist: Sees GenAI improving surgical safety and access, but notes an operating-room output can shape an irreversible act with seconds to catch errors.
Supports the competency approach but wants risk to weigh system authority, irreversibility, time to harm, detection opportunity and rescue capacity.
Wants premarket evaluation of the whole human-AI team in realistic workflows, covering rare events, degraded inputs, latency, automation bias and takeover.
Would refuse the premarket-for-postmarket trade for any function that can influence or execute an invasive, immediate or irreversible action.
Wants surveillance specific to model version, setting and subgroups, capturing near misses, overrides, abstentions, failed takeovers and drift.
Wants duties for manufacturers, model providers, institutions and clinicians proportionate to what each knows, controls, can prevent and gains from.
Wants foundation-model changes handled as safety-relevant supply-chain events.
Wants agentic systems to have explicit action and tool boundaries, confirmation steps, stop conditions, immutable logs, safe failure modes and takeover testing.
Wants access-expanding systems evaluated beyond wealthy academic centers, across populations, anatomy, rural settings, resource levels and user experience.
Says a framework that judges the deployed human-AI system and keeps someone responsible wherever control sits can protect the opportunity.
Sees the greatest surgical benefit when GenAI is integrated with operative video, robotics, digital operating rooms and telecollaboration.
Says a model built around informational outputs falls short for physical acts, so the unit of evaluation must be the human-AI team in its workflow.
Supports the competency approach with five refinements spanning added risk factors, team evaluation, no trade for invasive actions, surveillance and accountability.
Argues surgery's immediate, irreversible, seconds-to-detect, team-distributed risks justify explicit attention within the general framework.
Wants the two axes supplemented with irreversibility, time to harm, detection and rescue opportunity, system authority, review quality and environmental dependence.
Offers a five-step procedural continuum from observing to autonomous action, and warns a nominal clinician in the loop does not make a function low risk.
Wants realistic conversational and action trajectories evaluated for cumulative anchoring, overconfidence, premature closure and drift beyond intended use.
Wants the two escalation errors assessed apart from each other, since their harms cannot be traded one for one.
Finds the competency model useful only if competency refers to the whole device in its real environment, not a bare foundation model.
Lists benchmark elements including spatial reasoning, abstention, adversarial robustness, rare anatomy and faults, team communication, safe degradation and agentic boundaries.
Says public benchmarks alone are inadequate under contamination or weak validity; wants proof they predict workflow performance, with protected test sets.
Would allow retrospective or silent deployment for observational functions but require prospective evaluation under stress conditions for invasive ones.
Wants high-risk surgical confirmation to progress through simulation, cadaveric or preclinical work, staged introduction and prospective study, as in IDEAL.
Where a device supports a clinician, wants team evaluation measuring error recognition, automation bias, workload, takeover time, skill retention and experience effects.
Accepts a care-without-device comparator but wants an absolute safety floor so a poor local baseline cannot institutionalize substandard care.
Would let synthetic data supplement rare-event testing but not replace representative clinical data in procedural use, with real and synthetic results reported separately.
Wants third parties in high-risk benchmarking, confirmation, cybersecurity review and postmarket audit, with independence criteria including freedom to publish.
Finds more postmarket reliance reasonable only for reviewable, reversible, low-consequence functions, never where harm precedes review or rescue is uncertain.
Wants monitoring to capture versions, out-of-scope use, subgroup and site performance, overrides, near misses, interface failures, automation bias and case-mix shifts.
Wants cadence set by risk and reassessment triggered by model, workflow, hardware or population changes and unexpected signals.
Welcomes data from clinicians, institutions, registries and societies as long as participation does not diffuse manufacturer accountability.
Accepts supervisory agents as aids if their sensitivity, specificity, independence, failure modes and correlated-error risk are evaluated.
Wants contracts giving notice, version access and update suspension, technical blocks on unreviewed substitution, and FDA review of changes to authority or scope.
Finds master files useful if current, and asks FDA to consider expecting an adequate file whenever a device depends heavily on a third-party model.
Wants defined permitted actions, confirmation for consequential actions, validated stop states, immutable logs, sub-agent detection, safe degradation and takeover testing.
Would credit a human supervisor only when they have the training, attention, authority, information and time to intervene.
Would assign manufacturers design and monitoring, institutions local validation and credentialing, clinicians reasonable use, and model providers duties matching their control.
Wants documentation and labeling to expose who controls what, rather than letting contracts shift risk downstream.
Wants evidence across demographic groups, disease severity, community settings and resource levels, with aggregation not hiding subgroup failures.
Wants clinicians, patients and rural representatives involved early in defining intended use, endpoints, transparency and monitoring.
Wants regulation to protect the opportunity while placing firm safeguards where software begins to direct physical action.
Summarizes its asks for procedural uses: evaluate the deployed team, add authority and irreversibility to risk, require realistic confirmation and versioned evidence.
